topic: Telemetry Floods Crush Naive FHIR Pipelines
postText:
Converting continuous bedside telemetry directly into FHIR Observation resources will melt your healthcare database. In healthcare facilities where I work, bridging legacy HL7 v2 feeds with modern FHIR APIs taught us this painful lesson early.

Bedside monitors emit vitals at 100Hz to 500Hz. When ingestion workers naively map every waveform packet into distinct FHIR JSON resources and write them to an operational data store, IOPS explodes. Worse, mixing high-frequency waveform blobs with relational clinical records compromises both ingestion throughput and strict PHI isolation boundaries.

Here is the architecture pattern that stabilized our clinical pipeline:

1. Edge Aggregation: Place a local gateway beside device clusters to downsample raw waveforms into statistical summaries (mean, min, max, variance) across 5-second tumbling windows.
2. Dual-Path Storage: Stream high-resolution raw telemetry to an encrypted time-series engine. Emit only discrete clinical states, alerts, and aggregated trends into the FHIR server.
3. Zero-Trust Hardware Identity: Terminate device traffic via mutual TLS (mTLS) with device certificates. Strip direct patient identifiers at the boundary, routing pseudo-anonymized device IDs with cryptographic envelope encryption.

FHIR is built for interoperability and clinical state exchange, not sub-second waveform streaming. Decouple raw telemetry from your clinical document core.

How does your team handle high-frequency IoT or medical device ingestion without choking your transactional database?
